title: The Byrds in the 1960s
content:
1960s • ARTIST / BAND FEATURE

The Byrds

Folk Rock / Psychedelia / Country Rock

The Byrds electrified Dylan’s songs with a twelve-string Rickenbacker and vocal harmonies, then opened two different roads towards psychedelia and country rock.

MEET THE ARTIST

The story through the 1960s

The Byrds electrified Dylan’s songs with a twelve-string Rickenbacker and vocal harmonies, then opened two different roads towards psychedelia and country rock.

AN INTRODUCTION FROM OLDIES RADYO

It would be easy to tell the Byrds’s story through “Mr. Tambourine Man” alone. The more revealing story lies in the road to that recording and in the way the same sound changed over the years. Alongside the dates, we follow the person on stage, the decisions in the studio and the feeling that stays with the listener.

Folk meets rock in Los Angeles

Jim McGuinn, Gene Clark and David Crosby came from the folk clubs. With Chris Hillman and Michael Clarke joining them, the band brought the Beatles’ group model together with the American folk repertoire. McGuinn’s twelve-string Rickenbacker supplied the ringing foundation of the Byrds’ sound.

“Mr. Tambourine Man” turned Dylan’s long song into a short, gleaming pop single. Although studio musicians played on the recording, the band soon developed its own strengths in live performance and original songwriting.

Gene Clark and the early songwriting

Gene Clark was the early band’s most prolific writer, contributing emotionally direct songs such as “I’ll Feel a Whole Lot Better” and “Set You Free This Time”. Fear of flying, the pressures of touring and an unequal distribution of income contributed to his departure in 1966.

Their version of Pete Seeger’s “Turn! Turn! Turn!” kept folk rock’s mass success going. The Byrds were pioneers in taking traditional and contemporary words into the arrangements of electric pop.

Psychedelia and tensions in the line-up

“Eight Miles High”, with guitar lines influenced by John Coltrane and Ravi Shankar, became an early landmark of psychedelic rock. Fifth Dimension and Younger Than Yesterday brought studio experiments, space imagery and social observations into the band’s work.

David Crosby’s independent attitude and political speeches at Monterey Pop contributed to tensions within the band; he left in 1967. Michael Clarke departed not long afterwards.

The turn towards country rock

With Gram Parsons joining, Sweetheart of the Rodeo brought the country repertoire of Nashville and Bakersfield to rock listeners. Its immediate commercial reception was limited, but it came to be regarded as a foundational record for country rock and Americana.

McGuinn kept the band’s name going. Towards the end of the 1960s, Clarence White’s guitar playing opened a new chapter in technique and live performance.

The influence beyond the songs

The Byrds’ influence can be heard throughout jangle pop, folk rock, psychedelia and country rock. They connected the American band model that followed the Beatles with local folk and country roots.

The twelve-string guitar and the language of folk rock

As the Byrds brought Dylan’s songwriting into the post-Beatles group format, Roger McGuinn’s twelve-string Rickenbacker proved decisive. Its bright, bell-like tone became a signature of folk rock through “Mr. Tambourine Man”. Gene Clark’s introspective songs, David Crosby’s harmonic adventurousness and the band’s layered voices gave the early albums a powerful identity.

The use of Wrecking Crew musicians on the first single, within the Los Angeles studio system, prompted arguments about the band’s authenticity. Yet the Byrds soon developed their own abilities on stage and in the studio. “Turn! Turn! Turn!” joined biblical words to a modern longing for peace, while “Eight Miles High” opened the door to psychedelia through jazz and Indian influences.

Line-up changes and country rock

Clark’s fear of flying, the strain of touring and inequalities created by songwriting royalties contributed to his departure. Crosby’s political and musical independence deepened the line-up conflicts after Monterey Pop. Frequent personnel changes unsettled the Byrds, but they also helped push each incarnation towards a different musical territory.

Parsons’ brief involvement on Sweetheart of the Rodeo brought Nashville musicians and country songs before a rock audience. Initially met with suspicion in both country and rock circles, the album later became a cornerstone of country rock and Americana. The Byrds were among the few bands to build a direct bridge between folk rock, psychedelia and country rock.

AN OLDIES RADYO LISTENING NOTE

Getting to know The Byrds

Begin with Mr. Tambourine Man, which turned Dylan’s song into a worldwide manifesto for folk rock. Next, Eight Miles High reveals another colour in the band’s career. Finally, Hickory Wind takes the listening route towards its country conclusion in the 1960s.

The aim is to hear how the artist’s sound, interpretation and personality changed over time, rather than rush through a list of hits.

A LISTENING ROUTE THROUGH THE 1960s

Selected recordings for exploring the decade

This chronological selection follows the career’s direction, changes in sound and major turning points across the decade. It is a listening route rather than a ranking of the best songs. Individual recording features will be linked as they become available.

A high point of Gene Clark’s melodic and emotionally direct songwriting.

Made words drawn from scripture into a call for peace.

1966

A psychedelic rock pioneer, drawing on Coltrane and Indian music.

1967

title: Simon & Garfunkel in the 1960s
content:
1960s • ARTIST / BAND FEATURE

Simon & Garfunkel

Folk Pop / Harmony Pop

Paul Simon’s literary songs of city life and Art Garfunkel’s clear tenor gave the loneliness, failed communication and youthful feelings of the 1960s an elegant folk-pop voice.

MEET THE ARTIST

The story through the 1960s

Paul Simon’s literary songs of city life and Art Garfunkel’s clear tenor gave the loneliness, failed communication and youthful feelings of the 1960s an elegant folk-pop voice.

AN INTRODUCTION FROM OLDIES RADYO

It would be easy to tell Simon & Garfunkel’s story through “The Sound of Silence” alone. The more revealing story lies in the road to that recording and in the way the same sound changed over the years. Alongside the dates, we follow the person on stage, the decisions in the studio and the feeling that stays with the listener.

From Tom & Jerry to a folk duo

Paul Simon and Art Garfunkel began singing together as children and had a modest hit as Tom & Jerry in 1957. Their paths diverged during their university years, but the folk revival brought them back together.

When Wednesday Morning, 3 A.M. failed to find an audience in 1964, Simon went to England. Producer Tom Wilson added electric instruments to “The Sound of Silence” without the duo’s knowledge. Its success in 1965 brought them together again.

Folk-pop and city life

Sounds of Silence and Parsley, Sage, Rosemary and Thyme combined acoustic guitar, two-part harmonies and carefully detailed studio arrangements. “Homeward Bound”, “I Am a Rock” and “A Hazy Shade of Winter” put personal loneliness alongside lively pop structures.

Rather than broad political slogans, Simon’s songs concentrated on individual alienation, communication between generations and modern urban life. Garfunkel’s voice added a bright, fragile upper layer to Simon’s drier delivery.

The Graduate and mass success

Mike Nichols’ use of “The Sound of Silence”, “Scarborough Fair/Canticle” and the newly written “Mrs. Robinson” in The Graduate placed the duo at the centre of film and youth culture. “Mrs. Robinson” maintained a humorous distance from both the character and the era’s moral hypocrisy.

Bookends brought ageing, memory, city life and generational differences into a thematically connected album. Brief sound collages and studio experiments showed that the duo’s music reached beyond acoustic folk.

Personal tensions

Simon was the songwriter and the driving force behind the arrangements; Garfunkel was crucial to the vocals and public image. Creative credit, decision-making and Garfunkel’s move towards acting created tensions between them.

Recording for Bridge over Troubled Water began towards the end of the 1960s, although the album was released in 1970. As the decade closed, the duo’s artistic peak and personal separation were approaching together.

The influence beyond the songs

Simon & Garfunkel joined folk songwriting to expansive pop production. Their harmony model and urban melancholy left a lasting mark on generations of singer-songwriters and soft rock musicians.

The unexpected beginning of studio success

Simon and Garfunkel had sung together since childhood and recorded as Tom & Jerry in the 1950s. When Wednesday Morning, 3 A.M. initially attracted little attention, Simon went to England. Wilson’s addition of electric guitar, bass and drums to “The Sound of Silence”, without consulting the duo, placed the song within the folk rock wave and reunited its singers.

That unexpected success established a central tension in their career: simple two-part harmony alongside increasingly elaborate studio production. Simon’s words about urban loneliness, youthful alienation and the failure to communicate found an emotional clarity in Garfunkel’s clean tenor.

Film, the art of the album and personal tensions

Nichols’ use of their songs in The Graduate demonstrated how pop music could express a film character’s inner life. The new sections written for “Mrs. Robinson” allowed film and record success to feed each other. Bookends considered ageing, memory and American society through songs interspersed with brief sound collages.

Simon’s growing control as songwriter and production leader, together with Garfunkel’s acting projects, strained the relationship. Their perfectionist approach to recording nevertheless laid the groundwork for Bridge over Troubled Water. By the end of the 1960s, they offered one of the most graceful examples of the journey from folk-club simplicity to large-scale studio pop.

AN OLDIES RADYO LISTENING NOTE

Getting to know Simon & Garfunkel

Begin with The Sound of Silence and the unexpected transformation of an acoustic song through an electric arrangement. Then Scarborough Fair/Canticle reveals another side of their work. Finally, A Hazy Shade of Winter brings the route to one of their most forceful recordings of the 1960s.

The aim is to hear how the artist’s sound, interpretation and personality changed over time, rather than rush through a list of hits.

A LISTENING ROUTE THROUGH THE 1960s

Selected recordings for exploring the decade

This chronological selection follows the career’s direction, changes in sound and major turning points across the decade. It is a listening route rather than a ranking of the best songs. Individual recording features will be linked as they become available.

The unexpected transformation of an acoustic song through an electric arrangement.

1966

Turned the loneliness of touring into a melodic folk-pop standard.

1966

Described emotional self-defence in sharp, memorable words.

1966

Combined a traditional melody with an anti-war countermelody.

1968

1968

Made an American journey into a story of identity and searching.

1968

title: The Doors in the 1960s
content:
1960s • ARTIST / BAND FEATURE

The Doors

Psychedelic Rock / Blues Rock

The Doors joined Jim Morrison’s poetic, dangerous stage persona to Ray Manzarek’s keyboards, Robby Krieger’s guitar and John Densmore’s jazz-sensitive drumming.

MEET THE ARTIST

The story through the 1960s

The Doors joined Jim Morrison’s poetic, dangerous stage persona to Ray Manzarek’s keyboards, Robby Krieger’s guitar and John Densmore’s jazz-sensitive drumming.

AN INTRODUCTION FROM OLDIES RADYO

The Doors’ music holds the unease of a Los Angeles night rather than the warmth of its sunshine. Manzarek’s organ, Krieger’s guitar, Densmore’s jazz-rooted drums and Morrison’s theatrical darkness keep one another in a state of constant tension.

The beginnings in Los Angeles

Morrison and Manzarek knew each other through UCLA’s film community. The idea of turning Morrison’s poems, written at Venice Beach, into songs became a band. With Krieger and Densmore joining, the distinctive line-up took shape without a bass guitarist, using keyboard bass instead.

Their time on stage at the Whisky a Go Go developed the extended improvisations and Morrison’s theatrical storytelling. Being dismissed from the club over the Oedipal passage in “The End” reinforced their controversial identity from the beginning.

The first album and the breakthrough

The 1967 album The Doors set out their blend of blues, jazz, poetry and psychedelia through “Break On Through”, “Light My Fire” and “The End”. Krieger’s “Light My Fire”, with its extended, jazz-influenced middle passage from Manzarek and Densmore, took the album version beyond the boundaries of a single.

Their refusal to change the word “higher” on The Ed Sullivan Show became a symbol of their conflict with television censorship. Morrison rapidly emerged as one of rock’s most charismatic and unpredictable figures.

Productivity and darkness

Strange Days, Waiting for the Sun and The Soft Parade followed in quick succession. “People Are Strange”, “When the Music’s Over”, “Five to One” and “Touch Me” showed the band moving between dark cabaret, political unease and orchestral pop.

The strings and brass on The Soft Parade divided listeners. By the end of 1969, work on Morrison Hotel was bringing the band back towards a more direct blues-rock sound.

Miami and the pressure on the band

Morrison’s drinking and determination to push boundaries made concerts increasingly risky. Allegations of indecent conduct after the 1969 Miami show led to cancelled touring dates and placed the band’s public reputation under intense pressure.

The tension between Morrison’s seriousness as a poet and his image as a rock star sat at the heart of the story. The other three members tried to maintain musical discipline, but incidents on stage often overshadowed the recordings.

The influence beyond the songs

The Doors presented psychedelic rock as a dark theatre of death, desire, alienation and authority, extending well beyond the colourful pleasures of the counterculture. Their keyboard-led sound and Morrison’s poetic presence influenced later gothic and alternative rock.

Los Angeles, poetry and collective arrangements

The band’s dark identity came from more than Morrison’s stage personality. Manzarek’s classically and blues-influenced keyboards, Krieger’s guitar sources, including flamenco, and Densmore’s jazz sensibility created a broad sonic space without a bass guitarist. Songs often developed through collective arrangements in the rehearsal room.

The Sunset Strip clubs and their residency at the Whisky a Go Go allowed extended pieces to take shape before an audience. The difference between the shortened “Light My Fire” single and its long album version reflects changing expectations between 1960s radio formats and album listeners.

Censorship, stage crises and the Morrison myth

The refusal to alter “higher” on The Ed Sullivan Show strengthened their image as opponents of censorship. Morrison’s drinking, provocative monologues and clashes with police made concerts unpredictable. The case following the Miami concert in 1969 reflected society’s fear of rock stardom as well as disputes over what had actually happened on stage.

The mythology surrounding Morrison can obscure the other members’ contributions. The orchestral pop of “Touch Me”, the expansive arrangements on The Soft Parade and the band’s blues foundations all emerged from a collective search. The Doors embodied the dark, theatrical and potentially self-consuming side of the 1960s ideal of freedom.

AN OLDIES RADYO LISTENING NOTE

Getting to know The Doors

Begin with Break On Through (To the Other Side), the band’s opening manifesto of Latin rhythm and cutting vocals. Then move to People Are Strange for another side of their work. Finally, Touch Me takes the story towards their orchestral pop at the end of the 1960s.

The aim is to hear how the artist’s sound, interpretation and personality changed over time, rather than rush through a list of hits.

A LISTENING ROUTE THROUGH THE 1960s

Selected recordings for exploring the decade

This chronological selection follows the career’s direction, changes in sound and major turning points across the decade. It is a listening route rather than a ranking of the best songs. Individual recording features will be linked as they become available.

1967

Break On Through (To the Other Side)

The opening manifesto of the band, driven by Latin rhythm and cutting vocals.

1967

Joined a pop hit to an extended jazz-rock improvisation.

1967

The End

A dark culmination of poetry, drama and long-form composition.

1967

People Are Strange

Expressed alienation through a short, theatrical pop song.

1967

Joined stage improvisation to political and existential intensity.

1968

A brief, direct and controversial major hit.

1969

Touch Me

The orchestral pop side of the band, with brass and a strong melody.

title: Jimi Hendrix in the 1960s
content:
1960s • ARTIST / BAND FEATURE

Jimi Hendrix

Psychedelic Rock / Blues Rock

Jimi Hendrix was one of the 1960s’ most revolutionary musicians, redefining the electric guitar’s possibilities in tone, feedback, recording and performance within just a few years.

MEET THE ARTIST

The story through the 1960s

Jimi Hendrix was one of the 1960s’ most revolutionary musicians, redefining the electric guitar’s possibilities in tone, feedback, recording and performance within just a few years.

AN INTRODUCTION FROM OLDIES RADYO

Hendrix did more than play guitar louder: he removed the boundaries around what the instrument could become. Noise, feedback, blues phrases and a vulnerable voice could sound like a storm and a confession at the same time.

From the Chitlin’ Circuit to London

Born in Seattle, Hendrix worked after his military service as a supporting guitarist for Little Richard, the Isley Brothers and other R&B performers. Those years taught him professional stage discipline, although his experimental approach was often constrained when it drew attention from the lead singer.

While playing with Jimmy James and the Blue Flames in New York’s Greenwich Village, he was discovered by Chas Chandler, who brought him to London in 1966. The Jimi Hendrix Experience formed with Noel Redding and Mitch Mitchell.

The breakthrough in Britain

“Hey Joe”, “Purple Haze” and “The Wind Cries Mary” quickly put Hendrix at the centre of British rock. Musicians including Eric Clapton, Pete Townshend and Paul McCartney were struck by his command of the guitar.

Are You Experienced joined blues foundations to fuzz, feedback and studio experimentation. Across the work that followed, wah-wah and stereo techniques further expanded that language. Hendrix treated the guitar as an instrument for creating soundscapes as well as playing solos.

Monterey, Axis and Electric Ladyland

His appearance at the 1967 Monterey Pop Festival, ending with a burning guitar, marked a major breakthrough in the United States. The performance went beyond shock: his command of the stage, rhythm and tone reached a theatrical climax.

Axis: Bold as Love offered shorter, colourful and intricately shaped songs. With studio guests, extended blues improvisations and an intensive recording process, Electric Ladyland expressed his broadest vision. “All Along the Watchtower” transformed Dylan’s composition into a sonic architecture entirely his own.

Changing bands and Woodstock

Musical and personal tensions with Noel Redding contributed to the end of the Experience. Hendrix sought a direction more rooted in funk and R&B with Black musicians; the Band of Gypsys line-up took shape late in 1969.

His performance of the American national anthem at Woodstock became one of the era’s most powerful political interpretations, using guitar sounds that suggested sirens and explosions. Patriotism and protest could be heard within the same performance.

The influence beyond the songs

Hendrix’s impact extended far beyond displays of technique. He joined the feeling of blues to psychedelic sound design, making the studio, effects pedals and amplifier noise part of composition itself. The subsequent language of rock guitar is inseparable from those innovations.

From the Chitlin’ Circuit to London

In the first half of the 1960s, Hendrix played guitar with the Isley Brothers, Little Richard and various R&B groups. This gave him professional discipline, but his flamboyant playing often came into conflict with the main performer’s limits. Chandler’s discovery of him during his brief ventures as a bandleader in Greenwich Village completely changed the direction of his career.

The Experience, formed in London with Mitchell and Redding, brought blues foundations together with the British rock scene’s volume, fashion and recording experiments. That a Black American musician first became a star in Britain also exposed inequalities in the American music industry’s recognition of its own innovators.

Guitar language, the studio and identity

Hendrix used feedback, wah-wah, octave effects and the stereo field as elements of composition rather than decorative displays. The physical characteristics of the Stratocaster he reversed for left-handed playing affected its string feel and his use of the tremolo. Recordings with Eddie Kramer and producer Chandler demonstrated that layered guitars could tell a story as effectively as a voice.

Burning his guitar at Monterey made Hendrix highly visible in the United States, but he resisted being reduced to a stage sensation. The lengthy work on Electric Ladyland and the search that led towards Band of Gypsys reflected his wish for a more independent direction centred on Black music and funk. His Woodstock anthem became a wordless commentary on war, noise and national identity.

AN OLDIES RADYO LISTENING NOTE

Getting to know Jimi Hendrix

Begin with Hey Joe, which turned a song already in circulation into a dramatic debut single. Next, Little Wing reveals another colour in his playing. Finally, Star Spangled Banner (Woodstock) brings this 1960s route to his historic interpretation of the anthem.

The aim is to hear how the artist’s sound, interpretation and personality changed over time, rather than rush through a list of hits.

A LISTENING ROUTE THROUGH THE 1960s

Selected recordings for exploring the decade

This chronological selection follows the career’s direction, changes in sound and major turning points across the decade. It is a listening route rather than a ranking of the best songs. Individual recording features will be linked as they become available.

1966

Hey Joe

Turned a song already in circulation into a dramatic debut single.

1967

Purple Haze

Fuzz guitar, ambiguous words and a new psychedelic tone.

1967

The Wind Cries Mary

The gentle, melodic and economical side of Hendrix’s guitar.

1967

Little Wing

Concentrated harmony, colour and feeling into a brief recording.

1968

Voodoo Child (Slight Return)

A defining expression of his stage identity, with wah-wah and a towering riff.

1968

All Along the Watchtower

Made a Dylan interpretation into a studio masterpiece.

1969

Star Spangled Banner (Woodstock)

A historic reading that opened the national anthem to the sounds of war and protest.

Editor’s effects note: The Turkish source places wah-wah alongside the debut album’s techniques. This edition distinguishes the debut’s fuzz and feedback from the later use of wah-wah. The official Hendrix archive’s discussion of Electric Ladyland identifies the wah-wah part in “Burning of the Midnight Lamp”.

title: The Supremes in the 1960s
content:
1960s • ARTIST / BAND FEATURE

The Supremes

Motown / Pop Soul / Girl Group

Diana Ross, Florence Ballard and Mary Wilson formed the Supremes, whose elegant Motown pop transformed the worldwide visibility of Black women performers.

MEET THE ARTIST

The story through the 1960s

Diana Ross, Florence Ballard and Mary Wilson formed the Supremes, whose elegant Motown pop transformed the worldwide visibility of Black women performers.

AN INTRODUCTION FROM OLDIES RADYO

Behind the Supremes’ elegant image lay an extraordinarily demanding routine in the studio and on stage. Ross’s slender, almost conversational voice, Holland–Dozier–Holland’s songs and the Funk Brothers’ rhythms made them one of Motown’s brightest faces to the world.

The Primettes and the arrival at Motown

Formed in Detroit as a sister group to the Primes, the Primettes comprised Ballard, Wilson, Ross and, initially, Betty McGlown. Their persistent attempts to audition for Motown earned them experience inside the company through backing vocals, handclaps and similar supporting roles.

They signed as the Supremes in 1961. The first singles achieved little commercial success, and within the company they were jokingly called the “no-hit Supremes”. It was a long apprenticeship in stage presentation and studio discipline.

Holland–Dozier–Holland and the sequence of hits

“Where Did Our Love Go” became their first number one in 1964, followed by “Baby Love”, “Come See About Me”, “Stop! In the Name of Love” and “Back in My Arms Again”. Holland–Dozier–Holland’s short, rhythmic, melodic pop structures and Ross’s light but distinctive delivery formed a perfectly effective language for radio.

Choreography, specially designed stage clothes and television appearances strengthened their visual identity. The Supremes played a historic role in presenting Black women as elegant, central stars on mainstream American television.

Diana Ross at the centre and Florence Ballard

Motown chief Berry Gordy’s emphasis on Ross unsettled the balance within the group. Ballard’s powerful voice and role as a founder became increasingly overlooked. Health difficulties, a loss of confidence and company pressures contributed to her dismissal in 1967; Cindy Birdsong took her place.

The name changed to Diana Ross & the Supremes. Seen as preparation for Ross’s solo career, the decision also became the subject of lasting debate over the sidelining of Wilson’s and Ballard’s contributions.

The mature period and the parting

“You Keep Me Hangin’ On”, “Love Is Here and Now You’re Gone” and the psychedelic soul-influenced “Reflections” widened their sound. “Love Child” brought social stigma into mainstream pop.

In 1969, “Someday We’ll Be Together” became Ross’s final number one with the group. She began her solo career in 1970, while the Supremes continued with different line-ups.

The influence beyond the songs

Their achievements mattered beyond the charts, in representation, style and pop production. They joined the girl-group tradition to worldwide stardom and provided a fundamental model for later women’s groups.

The Motown system and visibility

The Supremes’ success emerged from the layered system at Hitsville U.S.A.: Holland–Dozier–Holland’s songs, the Funk Brothers’ rhythm tracks, Maxine Powell’s training in presentation and etiquette, choreography and meticulously prepared television costumes. Such professionalism could protect Black women entering discriminatory television and touring environments while also placing limits on them.

Ross’s light, conversational delivery, Ballard’s strong gospel-rooted voice and Wilson’s warm harmonies initially made a balanced trio. Production decisions favouring Ross altered that balance of power. The name Diana Ross and the Supremes made the tension between individual stardom and a group identity explicit.

Florence Ballard, expectations of women and the legacy

Ballard’s struggles with weight, mental health and discipline have often been presented simply as personal failings. Heavy touring, company control, unequal income and the experience of being pushed aside in a group she helped found make the picture more complicated. Her dismissal in 1967 shows the human cost behind Motown’s immaculate image.

By reaching white television audiences with an elegant presentation, the Supremes widened the boundaries of visibility during the civil rights era. Their staging, division of vocal roles and fashion also supplied a lasting model for later girl groups and women’s pop ensembles. Their success deserves to be measured through the worldwide redefinition of Black female stardom as well as the number of hits.

AN OLDIES RADYO LISTENING NOTE

Getting to know The Supremes

Begin with Where Did Our Love Go, the simple, irresistible single that launched the Motown hit sequence. Then You Can’t Hurry Love reveals another part of the story. Finally, Someday We’ll Be Together closes the listening route with the emotional farewell to the Diana Ross era.

The aim is to hear how the artist’s sound, interpretation and personality changed over time, rather than rush through a list of hits.

title: The Temptations in the 1960s
content:
1960s • ARTIST / BAND FEATURE

The Temptations

Motown / Vocal Soul / Psychedelic Soul

The Temptations became one of Motown’s longest-lasting and most musically adaptable groups through meticulously arranged voices, choreography and a succession of distinctive lead singers.

MEET THE ARTIST

The story through the 1960s

The Temptations became one of Motown’s longest-lasting and most musically adaptable groups through meticulously arranged voices, choreography and a succession of distinctive lead singers.

AN INTRODUCTION FROM OLDIES RADYO

It would be easy to tell the Temptations’s story through “The Way You Do the Things You Do” alone. The more revealing story lies in the road to that recording and in the way the same sound changed over the years. Alongside the dates, we follow the person on stage, the decisions in the studio and the feeling that stays with the listener.

Detroit vocal groups come together

Members from the Primes and the Distants came together as the Elgins, changing their name to the Temptations when they joined Motown. Otis Williams provided the group’s organisational backbone. Melvin Franklin’s deep bass and Paul Williams’ abilities on stage helped establish its early identity.

The first recordings achieved limited success. David Ruffin’s arrival in 1964 and Smokey Robinson’s “The Way You Do the Things You Do” brought the breakthrough.

The David Ruffin period

“My Girl” became their first number one, carried by Ruffin’s strong yet warm tenor and James Jamerson’s unforgettable bass line. “Ain’t Too Proud to Beg”, “Beauty Is Only Skin Deep” and “I Wish It Would Rain” placed Ruffin’s dramatic lead voice at the forefront.

Cholly Atkins’ choreography made their stage presentation a standard of Motown elegance. The sharing of lead and harmony roles among five distinct voices gave the repertoire great variety.

Ruffin’s departure and Dennis Edwards

Ruffin’s demands for solo-star treatment, missed appearances and refusal to follow group rules led to his dismissal in 1968. Dennis Edwards, formerly of the Contours, replaced him. The change coincided with a new period in Motown production, extending beyond the identity of the singer.

Norman Whitfield and Barrett Strong developed longer, more political and rhythmically ambitious recordings influenced by Sly and the Family Stone. “Cloud Nine” opened the psychedelic soul period as lead-vocal duties became more evenly distributed.

Psychedelic soul

“Runaway Child, Running Wild” and “I Can’t Get Next to You” expanded the classic Motown form with fuzz guitar, dense percussion and extended arrangements. The Temptations moved from elegant love songs towards city life and generational problems.

Paul Williams’ health difficulties and pressures within the group would become more severe in the following years. At the close of the 1960s, however, the band stood at the centre of Motown’s experimental transformation.

The influence beyond the songs

The Temptations joined vocal-group traditions to choreography, individual vocal character and continually renewed production. They became a foundational model for soul, funk and male vocal groups.

Five voices, choreography and Motown discipline

The group’s strength lay in the alternating use of different tenor and baritone colours rather than a single star. Eddie Kendricks’ high tenor, Ruffin’s rough-edged lead, Paul Williams’ emotional interpretations, Franklin’s deep bass and Otis Williams’ organisation could create a different dramatic centre in each song. Atkins’ choreography shaped the identity as decisively as the vocal arrangements.

Robinson’s “My Girl” brought out their warm, romantic side, while Whitfield moved towards harder rhythms and productions charged with social tension. The Funk Brothers’ studio playing, string and brass arrangements and immaculate stage clothes made the Temptations Motown’s ideal male group.

Line-up changes and psychedelic soul

Ruffin’s desire for solo stardom, behaviour problems and conflicts with group discipline resulted in his departure in 1968. Edwards brought a tougher gospel tone. At the same time, the influence of Sly and the Family Stone could be heard in the multiple leads, wah-wah guitar and denser rhythms of “Cloud Nine” and “I Can’t Get Next to You”.

This transformation demonstrated that the Temptations could reach well beyond romantic ballads. The Vietnam War, urban tensions and generational conflict provided a setting for later recordings. Their ability to retain an identity through changing personnel owed much to Otis Williams’ institutional memory and the Motown system’s capacity to rebuild.

AN OLDIES RADYO LISTENING NOTE

Getting to know The Temptations

Begin with The Way You Do the Things You Do, their first major hit and the opening of the Smokey Robinson period. Then I Wish It Would Rain reveals another side of the career. Finally, I Can’t Get Next to You takes the route towards the decade’s collective, funk-leaning finale.

The aim is to hear how the artist’s sound, interpretation and personality changed over time, rather than rush through a list of hits.

title: Marvin Gaye in the 1960s
content:
1960s • ARTIST / BAND FEATURE

Marvin Gaye

Motown / Soul / Pop

During the 1960s, Marvin Gaye developed from an elegant young Motown star into a more personal, vulnerable soul artist seeking control over his own work.

MEET THE ARTIST

The story through the 1960s

During the 1960s, Marvin Gaye developed from an elegant young Motown star into a more personal, vulnerable soul artist seeking control over his own work.

AN INTRODUCTION FROM OLDIES RADYO

It would be easy to tell Marvin Gaye’s story through “Stubborn Kind of Fellow” alone. The more revealing story lies in the road to that recording and in the way the same sound changed over the years. Alongside the dates, we follow the person on stage, the decisions in the studio and the feeling that stays with the listener.

Gospel roots and joining Motown

Raised in a strict religious household in Washington, D.C., Marvin Gay reached Detroit through doo-wop groups and his connection with Harvey Fuqua. At Motown he initially worked as a drummer and studio musician; he later added the “e” to his surname.

He first wanted to become a sophisticated singer of jazz standards in the mould of Nat King Cole. Berry Gordy directed him towards the young pop and R&B market instead. “Stubborn Kind of Fellow” and “Hitch Hike” were early successes in this new identity.

Motown stardom

“How Sweet It Is (To Be Loved by You)”, “I’ll Be Doggone” and “Ain’t That Peculiar” joined Gaye’s rhythmic but controlled delivery to the Funk Brothers’ studio discipline. His voice held the softness of a crooner as well as the fire of gospel.

Duets with Mary Wells, Kim Weston and, above all, Tammi Terrell brought Motown’s model of romantic dialogue to a peak. “Ain’t No Mountain High Enough” and “You’re All I Need to Get By” created a shared dramatic story through two independent voices.

VISUAL ARCHIVE

Marvin Gaye: stage presence through the years

Every image in this gallery shows the artist featured here. Pictures from different periods are placed together to illustrate changes across the career; no other performer is substituted.

Tammi Terrell and a personal turning point

Terrell’s collapse on stage in 1967 and treatment for a brain tumour deeply affected Gaye. Different accounts of the recording details emerged over the years, but her illness and death in 1970 intensified his depression.

Tensions with Motown management over artistic control were also growing. Gaye wanted to move beyond the role of a romantic hit singer, looking for more coherent works about war, city life and personal conflict.

I Heard It Through the Grapevine

Produced by Norman Whitfield, “I Heard It Through the Grapevine” became Gaye’s greatest success of the 1960s in 1968. Its dark arrangement, sense of paranoia and controlled tension revealed a more adult emotional world than his romantic image suggested.

The song’s success demonstrated that his dramatic vocal power could serve more experimental and personal productions. That direction prepared the ground for the major transformation of 1971.

The influence beyond the songs

For Gaye, the 1960s brought both stardom and a search for something further. Through duets, dance hits and dramatic ballads, he developed his vocal identity while moving towards a new role as an artist demanding control within the Motown system.

The tension between Motown stardom and artistic independence

Gaye entered Motown hoping to become an elegant crooner singing jazz standards; the company found a stronger market for him in rhythmic, romantic singles. “Hitch Hike”, “Can I Get a Witness” and “How Sweet It Is” joined gospel technique, dance rhythms and a smooth pop presentation. His background as a drummer could be heard in the flexible relationship between his vocal phrases and the beat.

His duets with Weston and particularly Terrell created the impression of a conversation unfolding in real time. Ashford & Simpson’s songs offered a form of romantic pop that was theatrical yet intimate. Terrell’s illness and collapse on stage in 1967 marked a deep break in Gaye’s personal and artistic world.

1968–69: looking inwards and asking new questions

Gladys Knight & the Pips had released “I Heard It Through the Grapevine” before Gaye’s version appeared. His darker, more controlled interpretation became a major success late in 1968. Whitfield’s tense arrangement amplified suspicion and paranoia through rhythm, revealing a singer capable of carrying complex feelings beyond his romantic persona.

His brother’s accounts of Vietnam, urban unrest, Terrell’s condition and conflicts with Motown’s production system pushed Gaye towards a more personal and socially engaged album. The full result would arrive in 1971, but its foundations were laid late in the 1960s. The decade therefore prepared his movement from stardom towards artistic autonomy.

AN OLDIES RADYO LISTENING NOTE

Getting to know Marvin Gaye

Begin with Stubborn Kind of Fellow, Gaye’s emphatic declaration of personality at Motown. Next, Ain’t No Mountain High Enough reveals another side of his career. Finally, Too Busy Thinking About My Baby brings the route to his continuing pop success at the end of the 1960s.

The aim is to hear how the artist’s sound, interpretation and personality changed over time, rather than rush through a list of hits.

title: Aretha Franklin in the 1960s
content:
1960s • ARTIST / BAND FEATURE

Aretha Franklin

Soul / Gospel / R&B

Aretha Franklin moved to the centre of soul in the second half of the 1960s, joining her gospel roots to a mature woman’s voice, command of the piano and a feeling of freedom.

MEET THE ARTIST

The story through the 1960s

Aretha Franklin moved to the centre of soul in the second half of the 1960s, joining her gospel roots to a mature woman’s voice, command of the piano and a feeling of freedom.

AN INTRODUCTION FROM OLDIES RADYO

Franklin did more than sing a song: she changed the balance of power within it. The piano and vocal language she brought from church could turn even everyday love songs into statements of freedom, respect and standing up for oneself.

Church, family and the early recordings

Growing up in the Detroit household of preacher C. L. Franklin, Aretha knew some of gospel’s greatest performers at close quarters. She played piano and sang at New Bethel Baptist Church as a child and made her first gospel recordings while still young.

Family life and becoming a mother at a very early age brought heavy responsibilities behind the career. With her father’s support, she turned towards secular music and signed with Columbia Records in 1960.

The Columbia years

John Hammond recognised her immense talent, but Columbia struggled to place her among jazz, pop standards, blues and orchestral arrangements. She made impressive recordings there, although her singular identity had yet to emerge fully.

Moments when Franklin accompanied herself on piano and used gospel phrases freely pointed towards the transformation to come. When her contract ended in 1966, Atlantic Records’ Jerry Wexler offered a setting that felt more natural to her.

VISUAL ARCHIVE

Aretha Franklin: stage presence through the years

Every image in this gallery shows the artist featured here. Pictures from different periods are placed together to illustrate changes across the career; no other performer is substituted.

Atlantic and the Muscle Shoals turning point

Recorded at FAME Studios in Muscle Shoals in 1967, “I Never Loved a Man (The Way I Love You)” brought her identity into focus through her piano, gospel intensity and a Southern rhythm section. The session was brief, but it established the direction of the Atlantic years.

She turned Otis Redding’s “Respect” into a statement of women’s self-esteem, sexual independence and a demand for social rights. The spelled-out refrain and the backing-vocal response became original elements of her interpretation.

Queen of Soul

“Chain of Fools”, “Think”, “(You Make Me Feel Like) A Natural Woman” and “Ain’t No Way” showed her range from forceful rhythm songs to vulnerable ballads. Her sisters Carolyn and Erma made important contributions through songwriting and vocals during this period.

Marital problems and pressure from work complicated Franklin’s private life. Yet she gained control on stage and in the studio. Playing piano, participating directly in arrangements and bringing her own experience to a song distinguished her from an ordinary interpreter.

The social and musical legacy

Family connections to the civil rights movement and her support for Martin Luther King Jr. joined the call for freedom in her music. Franklin placed Black women’s experience at the centre of mainstream pop and set technical, emotional and political standards for soul singing.

Gospel training and lessons from the Columbia years

In her father C. L. Franklin’s Detroit church, Aretha grew up close to Mahalia Jackson, Clara Ward and other leading gospel figures. Early recordings at the piano developed her improvisation, call-and-response and ability to make words personal as well as the power of her voice. Columbia placed her between jazz, pop standards and light R&B. These valuable recordings nevertheless fell short of capturing the full force of her identity.

Atlantic’s Jerry Wexler placed Franklin in an environment where she played her own piano, kept her gospel roots visible and worked with a more direct rhythm section. The first Muscle Shoals session was short, but “I Never Loved a Man” opened a new period. The recordings completed in New York built their arrangements around her voice instead of fitting it into a commercial mould.

Respect, women’s autonomy and performance

In rearranging Redding’s “Respect”, Franklin added the spelled-out refrain and the answering backing vocals. A male narrator’s demand for respect at home became a woman’s declaration of independence and reciprocity. The song became associated with civil rights and women’s movements, drawing its power from the everyday demand for equality within a relationship.

The vocal contributions of her sisters Carolyn and Erma, the circle around King Curtis and Atlantic’s players brought family and professional networks together in Franklin’s studio language. Violence in her private life, marriage and the pressure of relentless work were not always discussed openly, but they intertwined with the vulnerability and resistance of her interpretations. By the end of the 1960s, the title “Queen of Soul” expressed cultural authority as well as vocal range.

AN OLDIES RADYO LISTENING NOTE

Getting to know Aretha Franklin

Begin with Won’t Be Long, an early example of the gospel fire in her Columbia years. Then (You Make Me Feel Like) A Natural Woman reveals another side of the career. Finally, The Weight closes the 1960s route with a powerful gospel-soul interpretation.

The aim is to hear how the artist’s sound, interpretation and personality changed over time, rather than rush through a list of hits.

A LISTENING ROUTE THROUGH THE 1960s

This chronological selection follows the career’s direction, changes in sound and major turning points across the decade. It is a listening route rather than a ranking of the best songs. Individual recording features will be linked as they become available.

An early example of gospel fire in the Columbia years.

1967

The raw, intense soul recording that opened the Atlantic period.

1967

1967

Made the Carole King–Gerry Goffin song into a personal masterpiece.

1967

A major hit driven by sharp guitar and gospel call-and-response.

1968

Among her most direct statements as a songwriter on the theme of freedom.

title: James Brown in the 1960s
content:
1960s • ARTIST / BAND FEATURE

James Brown

Soul / Rhythm and Blues / Funk

James Brown became a principal architect of the move from soul to funk in the 1960s, combining stage discipline, rhythmic innovation and Black pride.

MEET THE ARTIST

The story through the 1960s

James Brown became a principal architect of the move from soul to funk in the 1960s, combining stage discipline, rhythmic innovation and Black pride.

AN INTRODUCTION FROM OLDIES RADYO

On stage, Brown was a conductor directing the pulse of the entire band as much as a singer. Shifting an accent, making the guitar work as rhythm rather than melody and turning dance into part of the music opened the door to funk.

The Famous Flames and the early struggle

Poverty in Georgia and South Carolina shaped Brown’s childhood and youth. His connection with Bobby Byrd around the end of his imprisonment led him into the gospel and R&B-based group that became the Famous Flames. “Please, Please, Please” brought a breakthrough in 1956.

Disagreements arose over the group’s name and division of income, while Brown quickly became its dominant star. By the early 1960s, constant touring, strict rehearsals and an unforgiving performance standard had established his identity as “The Hardest Working Man in Show Business”.

The live album and authority on stage

King Records executives doubted the idea of a live album at the Apollo Theater. Brown funded the recording himself; Live at the Apollo unexpectedly became a major, enduring success in 1963.

The stage show was built around falling to his knees, the cape ceremony, sudden rhythmic stops and carefully controlled tension with the audience. The Famous Flames and the orchestra had to respond instantly to Brown’s signals.

Rhythm moves to the centre

“Out of Sight”, “Papa’s Got a Brand New Bag” and “I Got You (I Feel Good)” developed an approach in which instruments worked as interlocking rhythmic cells more than melodic accompaniment. A powerful emphasis on the first beat became fundamental to funk.

With extended vamps, cutting guitars, syncopated bass and punctuating horns, “Cold Sweat” and “I Got the Feelin’” turned the soul song into a more abstract rhythmic machine. Contributions from Maceo Parker, Clyde Stubblefield and the other musicians were indispensable.

Black pride and a public role

The televised Boston concert following Martin Luther King Jr.’s assassination in 1968 is remembered as a historic moment that helped ease tensions in the city. Brown also used his public platform to stress Black economic independence and education.

“Say It Loud – I’m Black and I’m Proud” became one of popular music’s strongest expressions of Black pride through its children’s chorus and direct slogan. Brown’s politics did not always follow a single line, but his cultural influence was undeniable.

The influence beyond the songs

Brown’s approach to rhythm became a foundation for funk, disco and hip-hop. His drum breaks and brief vocal exclamations ranked among the sounds most widely used in the sampling culture that followed.

Stage discipline and the live album

The show developed with the Famous Flames depended on strict rehearsals, precise poses, the cape ritual and instantaneous commands to the band. Fining musicians for a wrong note or an error in their clothing could be seen as authoritarian. That discipline nevertheless allowed Brown to put his rhythmic ideas into practice with extraordinary precision. Funded by Brown despite the label’s doubts, the 1963 release Live at the Apollo demonstrated the commercial power of a live R&B album.

Brown began thinking of a song as interlocking rhythmic cells more than a sequence of chord changes. Drums, bass, guitar and horns became parts of a common groove instead of separate melodies. With their emphasis on the first beat, “Papa’s Got a Brand New Bag” and “Cold Sweat” established the grammar of funk.

Black pride, enterprise and contradictions

With its children’s chorus, “Say It Loud – I’m Black and I’m Proud” became an anthem that openly affirmed Black identity. Brown supported the televised Boston concert after King’s assassination in 1968, helping reduce tensions in the city. His relationships with conservative politicians and emphasis on order also made it difficult to place him within a single political position.

He championed Black enterprise through radio stations, restaurants and production companies, while disputes over pay and control strained relationships with his musicians. Those contradictions do not diminish his historical impact, but they reveal a gap between the language of freedom on stage and a severe workplace hierarchy. By the end of the 1960s, his rhythmic revolution had laid foundations for soul, funk, Afrobeat, disco and hip-hop.

AN OLDIES RADYO LISTENING NOTE

Getting to know James Brown

Begin with Think, full of the fast gospel-R&B energy of the Famous Flames years. Then Papa’s Got a Brand New Bag reveals another part of the career. Finally, Funky Drummer, recorded in 1969 and released in 1970, carries the route across the decade’s boundary.

The aim is to hear how the artist’s sound, interpretation and personality changed over time, rather than rush through a list of hits.

A LISTENING ROUTE THROUGH THE 1960s

This chronological selection follows the career’s direction, changes in sound and major turning points across the decade. It is a listening route rather than a ranking of the best songs. Individual recording features will be linked as they become available.

title: Otis Redding in the 1960s
content:
1960s • ARTIST / BAND FEATURE

Otis Redding

Southern Soul / Rhythm and Blues

Otis Redding became one of Southern soul’s greatest voices through gospel intensity, direct songwriting and an overwhelming stage presence. His career ended tragically in 1967.

MEET THE ARTIST

The story through the 1960s

Otis Redding became one of Southern soul’s greatest voices through gospel intensity, direct songwriting and an overwhelming stage presence. His career ended tragically in 1967.

AN INTRODUCTION FROM OLDIES RADYO

It would be easy to tell Otis Redding’s story through “These Arms of Mine” alone. The more revealing story lies in the road to that recording and in the way the same sound changed over the years. Alongside the dates, we follow the person on stage, the decisions in the studio and the feeling that stays with the listener.

From Macon to Memphis

Growing up in Macon, Georgia, Redding was inspired by Little Richard’s energy on stage and sang in gospel and R&B settings from a young age. Working as a driver and supporting singer with Johnny Jenkins’ band brought him into the Stax circle in Memphis.

“These Arms of Mine”, recorded at the end of a 1962 session, attracted attention through its slow, heartfelt vocal. Stax/Volt, with the support of Booker T. & the M.G.’s and the Memphis horns, brought his natural delivery forward without elaborate orchestral display.

Developing as a singer and songwriter

“Pain in My Heart”, “Mr. Pitiful”, “I’ve Been Loving You Too Long” and “Respect” showed his strength as a writer of rhythmic soul as well as powerful ballads. Repetition, a rising voice and economical words created intense emotional tension.

The original “Respect” made a demand from a man’s perspective; Franklin later transformed it into a very different anthem of freedom. The two interpretations provide a powerful example of a song’s changing ownership and meaning within soul.

Stage performance and Europe

In fast performances, Redding bent at the knees, sweated and directed the horns, making a direct connection with his audience. The Stax/Volt European tour demonstrated Black American soul’s enormous impact on British and European listeners.

His brief, intense set before the largely white rock audience at the 1967 Monterey Pop Festival introduced him to the counterculture generation. It marked the opening of a new phase in his career.

The final recordings and tragedy

After vocal-cord surgery, Redding explored a more controlled, melodic direction. Written with Steve Cropper, “(Sittin’ On) The Dock of the Bay” differed from his earlier work through its open structure, closing whistle and sense of stillness.

On 10 December 1967, Redding and most of the Bar-Kays travelling with him died when their touring aircraft crashed in Wisconsin. The song was released in 1968 and reached number one after his death.

The influence beyond the songs

Brief as his career was, Redding set a standard for Southern soul singing. His bridge between rock festival audiences and the Black R&B tradition symbolised the musical convergences of the 1960s.

The Stax family and the art of interpretation

Redding’s voice gained its power through the physical expression of feeling more than technical smoothness. Working in Stax’s Memphis studio with Booker T. & the M.G.’s, the Mar-Keys horns, producer Jim Stewart and Cropper kept the sound of a live band within the songs. Redding often developed new words and vocal outbursts in rehearsal, while Cropper shaped the ideas into song form.

“These Arms of Mine”, “I’ve Been Loving You Too Long” and “Try a Little Tenderness” demonstrated his ability to build intensity from a slow beginning. He was also a songwriter whose compositions, including “Respect”, had strong dramatic centres that other performers could transform.

Monterey, reaching new audiences and the unfinished future

The short Monterey set in 1967 showed Southern soul’s stage power to a largely white rock audience. Afterwards, Redding wanted to broaden his repertoire and writing, learning from the Beatles’ studio experiments and Dylan’s approach to words. “(Sittin’ On) The Dock of the Bay” offered a calmer, reflective and open-ended narrative than his earlier call-and-response explosions.

The December 1967 plane crash took Redding’s life and those of most of the touring musicians aboard. The song’s huge posthumous success reminds us that listeners heard only the beginning of his new direction. His legacy lived through Stax’s communal approach to recording, his open expression of male vulnerability and his bringing soul to the rock festival audience.

AN OLDIES RADYO LISTENING NOTE

Getting to know Otis Redding

Begin with These Arms of Mine, his first major Stax breakthrough and the emergence of a vulnerable ballad voice. Next, Respect reveals another side of the career. Finally, (Sittin’ On) The Dock of the Bay brings the route to the masterpiece that revealed a new direction after his death.

The aim is to hear how the artist’s sound, interpretation and personality changed over time, rather than rush through a list of hits.

A LISTENING ROUTE THROUGH THE 1960s

Selected recordings for exploring the decade

This chronological selection follows the career’s direction, changes in sound and major turning points across the decade. It is a listening route rather than a ranking of the best songs. Individual recording features will be linked as they become available.

1962

These Arms of Mine

The first major Stax breakthrough and the emergence of a vulnerable ballad voice.

1964

Mr. Pitiful

Joined humour and hurt within rhythmic soul.

1965

I’ve Been Loving You Too Long

A masterpiece of steadily rising vocal intensity.

1965

Respect

The forceful, demanding original that preceded Franklin’s interpretation.

1966

Try a Little Tenderness

A stage classic moving from a slow beginning to an explosive finale.

1967

Tramp

A playful, competitive duet with Carla Thomas.

1967/68

(Sittin’ On) The Dock of the Bay

The posthumously released masterpiece that revealed his new direction.
